chunks.text: 2.1 Context-Aware Segmentation Architectures Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), particularly U-Net and its variants, are the foundation of medical image segmentation due to their ability to extract local texture features [ 6 ] . The symmetric encoder-decoder structure with skip connections preserves spatial details, which helps delineate the often ill-defined boundaries of thyroid nodules [ 18 ] . However, the locality of convolutional operations limits the effective receptive field, making it difficult to capture long-range anatomical dependencies and global semantic context [ 19 ] . Although methods like Attention U-Net attempt to expand the receptive field, they often rely on local attention windows, which may not fully capture irregular nodule morphologies [ 20 ] . Consequently, CNN-based methods can struggle to distinguish nodules from surrounding tissues with similar echogenicity when global shape cues are missing [ 21 ] . To address the constraints of fixed receptive fields, Vision Transformers (ViTs) and their hybrid variants have been rapidly adopted to use global self-attention mechanisms for medical image segmentation [ 10 ] . By modeling the relationships between all image patches, architectures such as TransUNet and Swin-Unet can effectively capture long-range anatomical dependencies, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of the global shape and structural context of lesions [ 13 , 14 ] . This capability is theoretically advantageous for thyroid ultrasound segmentation, where the nodule’s global shape often provides the most reliable cue against complex backgrounds. Furthermore, channel-wise cross-attention and multi-resolution feature synchronization have been used to bridge semantic gaps between encoder and decoder layers and strengthen multi-scale fusion [ 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 ] .

These Transformer-based approaches demonstrate superior performance in scenarios requiring global semantic reasoning, moving beyond the inductive bias of locality that characterizes standard CNNs [ 26 ] . Despite their global modeling capabilities, Transformer-based architectures have limitations in ultrasound imaging. The global self-attention mechanism treats all spatial tokens equally, potentially aggregating information from noisy background regions such as speckle artifacts, shadowing, or surrounding glandular tissues [ 27 ] . This mixing of context can be detrimental in ultrasound images, where nodule-background contrast is low and acoustic noise is common, leading to boundary blurring or false positives [ 28 ] . Moreover, the computational cost of quadratic self-attention often requires downsampling or token pruning, risking the loss of local details essential for boundary delineation [ 29 ] . Consequently, current methods face a trade-off: while Transformers excel at global semantic understanding, they often lack the robustness to local noise found in CNNs. This highlights the need for architectures that selectively filter global context before fusing it with local geometric features [ 30 ] . 3 Method 3.1 Overview of SDFA-Net Architecture SDFA-Net addresses thyroid nodule segmentation challenges by balancing local boundary delineation with global semantic understanding. As shown in Figure 1 , our framework uses a dual-path architecture with a high-resolution local CNN branch and a context-aware global branch. The local branch, using a ResNet-34 backbone [ 39 ] , preserves spatial details critical for tracing irregular nodule boundaries. Meanwhile, the global branch processes downsampled features to capture long-range anatomical dependencies and the overall thyroid context. Figure 1: Overall architecture of SDFA-Net.

The model employs a dual-path design: a local path (blue) extracts high-resolution features, while a global context path (orange) captures long-range dependencies. The core ’filter-then-align’ strategy consists of (1) Clustered Linear Context Aggregation and Prototype Modulation to filter semantically irrelevant features, and (2) Spatially-Aligned Feature Fusion to deformably align global context with local boundaries before decoding. Our core contribution is the Semantic-Aware Deformable Feature Alignment pipeline, which uses a "filter-then-align" strategy. Instead of directly fusing raw multi-scale features—which often causes spatial misalignment and background noise interference—our approach first refines the global context using dynamic class prototypes. It then aligns the refined semantic priors with local features using learned deformable offsets. This two-stage process ensures that the final fusion integrates only semantically relevant information that is spatially registered to the local geometry. In the first stage, the global branch transforms deep convolutional features into a sequence of tokens and applies a Clustered Linear Context Aggregation module to efficiently capture long-range dependencies with linear computational complexity. By grouping semantically similar tokens into learnable cluster centroids, this module approximates the effect of full self-attention while avoiding its quadratic cost. The resulting globally enriched tokens encode anatomical context spanning the entire thyroid region. However, these tokens may still contain interference from surrounding tissues and acoustic artifacts prevalent in ultrasound imaging. To address this, an Affinity-Driven Token Modulation mechanism uses dynamically computed class prototypes to filter out background noise.

By calculating the semantic affinity of each token to the foreground nodule prototype, the module selectively suppresses irrelevant features while preserving those characteristic of the target structure. Following semantic filtering, the refined global features must be integrated with the high-resolution local features extracted by the CNN backbone. Direct concatenation or addition assumes rigid spatial correspondence, which fails for thyroid nodules exhibiting irregular and deformable shapes. To overcome this limitation, the Spatially-Aligned Feature Fusion module employs a cascaded alignment strategy. It utilizes a hierarchical offset prediction network to estimate dense deformation fields at multiple scales. These content-aware offsets guide a differentiable bilinear sampling operation that iteratively warps the semantic context to align with the precise geometry encoded in multi-level local features. This deformable alignment ensures that semantic priors from the global path are geometrically consistent with boundary details from the local path at each resolution level. The network is trained end-to-end using a composite loss function that combines pixel-level segmentation supervision with a prototype-based contrastive regularization. The segmentation loss employs both Binary Cross-Entropy and Dice loss to handle the severe class imbalance common in medical image segmentation. The prototype loss enforces semantic discriminability by pulling foreground tokens toward the foreground prototype while pushing background tokens away from the background prototype in the feature space. This dual supervision mechanism ensures that the network not only produces accurate segmentation masks but also learns a robust and semantically meaningful representation that supports effective noise filtering. The detailed formulation and implementation of each component are described in the following subsections.

3.2 Dual-Path Feature Extraction and Context Aggregation Accurate segmentation of thyroid nodules demands a balance between high-resolution boundary delineation and comprehensive global context understanding. To achieve this, we employ a multi-scale dual-path extraction strategy based on a ResNet-34 backbone [ 39 ] . The local path utilizes a feature pyramid extracted from multiple stages of the encoder with strides of 32, 16, 8, and 4, ensuring the preservation of fine-grained spatial details essential for tracing irregular nodule margins. Conversely, the global context path processes the deepest feature map from the final stage with a stride of 32. This lower-resolution input is subjected to average pooling, which significantly reduces the spatial dimensionality and computational load. By decoupling the paths, we maintain the geometric fidelity of multi-scale local features { F l ​ 1 , F l ​ 2 , F l ​ 3 } \{F_{l1},F_{l2},F_{l3}\} while enabling the global branch to efficiently capture long-range anatomical dependencies from the downsampled representation F l ​ o ​ w ∈ ℝ C × H 32 × W 32 F_{low}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times H_{32}\times W_{32}} . Although the global branch provides semantic context, standard self-attention mechanisms have O ⁡ ( N 2 ) O(N^{2}) computational complexity [ 40 ] . To address this, we introduce the Clustered Linear Context Aggregation (CLCA) module, which reduces complexity to linear O ⁡ ( N ​ K ​ C ) O(NKC) , where K K is the number of learnable cluster centroids and C C is the channel dimension. By grouping semantically similar tokens into clusters, we compress global information efficiently. The module calculates affinities only between tokens and learnable cluster centroids M ∈ ℝ K × C M\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times C} , modeling anatomical structures like nodule shape and position without the overhead of full self-attention.

The mathematical formulation of the CLCA module begins by computing the affinity matrix A ∈ ℝ N × K A\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times K} between the input tokens X ∈ ℝ N × C X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C} and the cluster centroids. We employ a differentiable Sinkhorn-Knopp normalization process to generate this affinity matrix. The doubly stochastic property enforced by the Sinkhorn algorithm ensures balanced assignments, preventing the collapse of clusters and significantly aiding the stability and convergence of the training process [ 41 ] . Formally, the initial affinity score A ~ i ​ j \tilde{A}_{ij} is derived from the scaled dot-product similarity: A ~ i ​ j = exp ⁡ ( X i ​ M j ⊤ / τ ) ∑ k = 1 K exp ⁡ ( X i ​ M k ⊤ / τ ) , \tilde{A}_{ij}=\frac{\exp(X_{i}M_{j}^{\top}/\tau)}{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\exp(X_{i}M_{k}^{\top}/\tau)}, (1) where τ \tau is a learnable temperature parameter. The final affinity matrix is obtained as A = Sinkhorn ​ ( A ~ ) A=\text{Sinkhorn}(\tilde{A}) . Using this matrix, the aggregated feature for the j j -th cluster centroid M ^ j \hat{M}_{j} is computed as the weighted sum of all input tokens assigned to it: M ^ j = ∑ i = 1 N A i ​ j ​ X i . \hat{M}_{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}A_{ij}X_{i}. (2) To reconstruct the global context for each individual token, the aggregated cluster features are broadcast back to the token space: G i = ∑ j = 1 K A i ​ j ​ M ^ j . G_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{K}A_{ij}\hat{M}_{j}. (3) Finally, the enhanced global tokens are produced via a residual connection: X g ​ l ​ o ​ b ​ a ​ l = X + G . X_{global}=X+G. (4) Following the context aggregation, the extracted local features F l F_{l} and the enhanced global tokens X g ​ l ​ o ​ b ​ a ​ l X_{global} must be integrated to support the final segmentation prediction.

To prepare for the subsequent alignment and fusion steps, the global tokens X g ​ l ​ o ​ b ​ a ​ l X_{global} are reshaped back into a 2D feature map F g ∈ ℝ C × H 32 × W 32 F_{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times H_{32}\times W_{32}} and upsampled via bilinear interpolation to match the spatial resolution of the local features ( H 16 × W 16 H_{16}\times W_{16} ). The fusion mechanism is initialized by concatenating the local and global feature maps along the channel dimension: F c ​ o ​ n ​ c ​ a ​ t = [ F l ; F u ​ p ] , F_{concat}=[F_{l};F_{up}], (5) where F u ​ p F_{up} denotes the upsampled global features. This concatenated representation serves as the input for the deformable alignment module, which learns to spatially warp the global context to align with local boundaries before generating the final output. Figure 2: Clustered Linear Context Aggregation (CLCA) module. The module groups semantically similar tokens into learnable cluster centroids via Sinkhorn normalization, capturing global anatomical context with linear computational complexity O ⁡ ( N ​ K ​ C ) O(NKC) . The doubly stochastic affinity matrix ensures balanced cluster assignments, and aggregated features are broadcast back to reconstruct global context for each token. 3.3 Affinity-Driven Token Modulation Although clustered context aggregation captures long-range dependencies, global tokens may still encode irrelevant information from surrounding tissues like muscles or the trachea. To ensure only semantically meaningful features contribute to segmentation, we introduce an Affinity-Driven Token Modulation mechanism. This module filters background noise while amplifying nodule-related features. We use class-specific prototypes as anchors to compute the semantic affinity of each token. As shown in Figure 3 , this process involves dynamically generating prototypes, calculating affinity scores, and applying a learned gating function to refine the global context.

To achieve robust semantic guidance, we compute class prototypes dynamically for each input image during training, using the ground truth mask Y g ​ t Y_{gt} . Unlike static learnable prototypes [ 42 ] , dynamic prototypes adapt to the specific anatomy and appearance of each scan, resolving potential circular dependencies in training. Let X g ​ l ​ o ​ b ​ a ​ l ∈ ℝ N × C X_{global}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C} denote the set of global tokens, where N N is the number of tokens and C C is the feature dimensionality. We first apply L2 normalization to the token vectors to obtain X ^ g ​ l ​ o ​ b ​ a ​ l \hat{X}_{global} , ensuring that the affinity calculation focuses on semantic direction rather than magnitude. The foreground prototype P f P_{f} and background prototype P b P_{b} are then computed via masked average pooling over their respective spatial regions. Mathematically, the class-specific prototypes are defined as: P c = 1 | Ω c | ​ ∑ i ∈ Ω c X ^ g ​ l ​ o ​ b ​ a ​ l , i , c ∈ { f , b } P_{c}=\frac{1}{|\Omega_{c}|}\sum_{i\in\Omega_{c}}\hat{X}_{global,i},\quad c\in\{f,b\} (6) where Ω f = { i ∣ Y g ​ t , i = 1 } \Omega_{f}=\{i\mid Y_{gt,i}=1\} represents the set of spatial indices belonging to the foreground nodule region, and Ω b = { i ∣ Y g ​ t , i = 0 } \Omega_{b}=\{i\mid Y_{gt,i}=0\} denotes the background region. Once the prototypes are established, we compute the semantic affinity of each global token to the foreground prototype and directly transform it into a gating coefficient. By using the L2-normalized vectors, the affinity score is computed using the dot product, which is equivalent to the cosine similarity measure.

We then pass this score through a sigmoid activation function σ \sigma , parameterized by learnable scalars α \alpha and β \beta , to obtain the gating coefficient g i g_{i} for the i i -th token: g i = σ ⁡ ( α ⋅ ( X ^ g ​ l ​ o ​ b ​ a ​ l , i ⋅ P f ⊤ ) + β ) g_{i}=\sigma\left(\alpha\cdot(\hat{X}_{global,i}\cdot P_{f}^{\top})+\beta\right) (7) Here, the dot product X ^ g ​ l ​ o ​ b ​ a ​ l , i ⋅ P f ⊤ \hat{X}_{global,i}\cdot P_{f}^{\top} quantifies the degree of semantic relatedness between the token and the nodule region. The scaling factor α \alpha adjusts the sensitivity of the gate, effectively sharpening or softening the decision boundary between foreground and background, while the bias term β \beta shifts the threshold to allow the network to learn a prior preference for foreground or background activation. The final modulated token X r ​ e ​ f ​ i ​ n ​ e ​ d , i X_{refined,i} is obtained by multiplying the original token X g ​ l ​ o ​ b ​ a ​ l , i X_{global,i} by the gating coefficient: X r ​ e ​ f ​ i ​ n ​ e ​ d , i = g i ⋅ X g ​ l ​ o ​ b ​ a ​ l , i X_{refined,i}=g_{i}\cdot X_{global,i} (8) This operation suppresses tokens with low affinity (likely background) and preserves those with high affinity (likely nodule), resulting in a purified global context representation. During inference, the ground truth mask Y g ​ t Y_{gt} is unavailable, precluding the online calculation of dynamic prototypes. To address this, we maintain a running average of the foreground and background prototypes observed during the training phase. We update the prototype memory using an exponential moving average with a momentum coefficient μ \mu . This allows the model to generalize the learned semantic centroids to unseen data without requiring test-time annotations.

The use of L2 normalization prior to affinity computation is essential, as it decouples the gating mechanism from variations in feature magnitude caused by different image contrasts or acquisition protocols, ensuring that the modulation relies solely on the semantic direction of the tokens. Consequently, the refined global features fed to the subsequent fusion module are highly discriminative and free from distracting background artifacts. Figure 3: Affinity-Driven Token Modulation mechanism. Dynamic class prototypes ( P f P_{f} for foreground, P b P_{b} for background) are computed from L2-normalized global tokens using ground truth masks during training. Semantic affinity scores between each token and the foreground prototype are converted into gating coefficients via a learnable sigmoid function. These coefficients selectively suppress background tokens while preserving foreground features, producing semantically purified global context. 3.4 Spatially-Aligned Feature Fusion Multi-scale feature integration is often hindered by spatial discrepancies between high-resolution local maps and coarse global context. Global features possess semantic priors but lack the geometric detail to delineate irregular boundaries. To bridge this gap, we propose a Spatially-Aligned Feature Fusion module that operates in a coarse-to-fine cascade. This module iteratively aligns and fuses high-level semantic features with multi-scale local features (strides 16, 8, and 4), inspired by feature pyramid networks and optical flow estimation [ 17 ] . We treat feature fusion as a hierarchical content-aware warping task. By predicting dense 2D offset fields at each resolution stage, we allow the global semantic context to deform adaptively, aligning its structures with the fine-grained geometry of local features. This is particularly important for thyroid nodules with spiculated or lobulated margins, where rigid transformations fail. Figure 4 illustrates the alignment mechanism at each stage.

Let { F l ​ 1 , F l ​ 2 , F l ​ 3 } \{F_{l1},F_{l2},F_{l3}\} denote the multi-scale local features extracted at strides 4, 8, and 16, respectively. The alignment process begins with the refined global feature map F g F_{g} (stride 32) and proceeds in a top-down manner. We define F f ​ u ​ s ​ e ​ d ( 4 ) = F g F_{fused}^{(4)}=F_{g} as the initial semantic prior. For each stage k ∈ { 3 , 2 , 1 } k\in\{3,2,1\} corresponding to strides { 16 , 8 , 4 } \{16,8,4\} , the fusion process involves three steps: upsampling, offset prediction, and deformable warping. First, the fused feature from the previous stage F f ​ u ​ s ​ e ​ d ( k + 1 ) F_{fused}^{(k+1)} is upsampled by a factor of 2 via bilinear interpolation to match the spatial resolution of the current local feature F l ​ k F_{lk} . An offset prediction network ϕ k \phi_{k} then estimates a dense displacement field Δ k \Delta_{k} based on the concatenation of the local feature and the upsampled semantic prior: Δ k = ϕ k ​ ( [ F l ​ k ; Up ​ ( F f ​ u ​ s ​ e ​ d ( k + 1 ) ) ] ) . \Delta_{k}=\phi_{k}([F_{lk};\text{Up}(F_{fused}^{(k+1)})]). (9) The network ϕ k \phi_{k} consists of two convolutional layers, predicting 2-channel offsets ( Δ ​ x , Δ ​ y ) (\Delta x,\Delta y) for each pixel. Using this offset field, we employ a differentiable bilinear sampling mechanism to warp the semantic prior, generating the aligned feature F ^ s ​ e ​ m ​ a ​ n ​ t ​ i ​ c ( k ) \hat{F}_{semantic}^{(k)} : F ^ s ​ e ​ m ​ a ​ n ​ t ​ i ​ c ( k ) ​ ( p ) = Sampler ​ ( Up ​ ( F f ​ u ​ s ​ e ​ d ( k + 1 ) ) , p + Δ k ​ ( p ) ) . \hat{F}_{semantic}^{(k)}(p)=\text{Sampler}(\text{Up}(F_{fused}^{(k+1)}),p+\Delta_{k}(p)). (10) Finally, the aligned semantic feature is fused with the local feature to produce the integrated representation for the current stage: F f ​ u ​ s ​ e ​ d ( k ) = Conv 3 × 3 ​ ( ReLU ​ ( Conv 1 × 1 ​ ( [ F l ​ k ; F ^ s ​ e ​ m ​ a ​ n ​ t ​ i ​ c ( k ) ] ) ) ) .

F_{fused}^{(k)}=\text{Conv}_{3\times 3}(\text{ReLU}(\text{Conv}_{1\times 1}([F_{lk};\hat{F}_{semantic}^{(k)}]))). (11) This cascaded process ensures that semantic priors are accurately registered to local details at each resolution level. The final output F f ​ u ​ s ​ e ​ d ( 1 ) F_{fused}^{(1)} at stride 4 serves as the input to the segmentation head, enabling precise boundary delineation even for small and irregular nodules. An offset prediction network ϕ \phi takes the concatenation of local features F l F_{l} and upsampled semantic features to predict a dense 2D offset field Δ \Delta . This field guides differentiable bilinear sampling to deformably warp the semantic features, producing aligned features that are geometrically registered to the local boundary details. This process is applied hierarchically across strides 16, 8, and 4. 3.5 Loss Function and Training Objective To train the proposed SDFA-Net end-to-end, we formulate a composite objective function that addresses both pixel-level accuracy and the semantic discriminability of the intermediate features. Thyroid ultrasound segmentation is characterized by a severe class imbalance, where the nodule region often occupies a significantly smaller area than the background tissue. To ensure robust convergence and prevent the model from being biased toward the background class, we employ a hybrid segmentation loss ℒ s ​ e ​ g \mathcal{L}_{seg} that combines the complementary benefits of Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) and the Dice similarity coefficient [ 43 ] . The BCE loss provides stable gradients by evaluating pixel-wise probabilities independently, while the Dice loss directly optimizes the overlap metric, making the model highly sensitive to the shape and boundary of the nodule.

Formally, let Y ^ ∈ ℝ H × W \hat{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W} denote the predicted probability map generated by the decoder, and let Y g ​ t ∈ { 0 , 1 } H × W Y_{gt}\in\{0,1\}^{H\times W} be the corresponding ground truth binary mask. The segmentation loss is defined as: ℒ s ​ e ​ g = ℒ b ​ c ​ e ​ ( Y ^ , Y g ​ t ) + ℒ d ​ i ​ c ​ e ​ ( Y ^ , Y g ​ t ) , \mathcal{L}_{seg}=\mathcal{L}_{bce}(\hat{Y},Y_{gt})+\mathcal{L}_{dice}(\hat{Y},Y_{gt}), (12) where the BCE term is computed as: ℒ b ​ c ​ e = − 1 H ​ W ∑ i = 1 H ​ W [ Y g ​ t , i log ( Y ^ i ) + ( 1 − Y g ​ t , i ) log ( 1 − Y ^ i ) ] , \mathcal{L}_{bce}=-\frac{1}{HW}\sum_{i=1}^{HW}\left[Y_{gt,i}\log(\hat{Y}_{i})+(1-Y_{gt,i})\log(1-\hat{Y}_{i})\right], (13) and the Dice loss is given by: ℒ d ​ i ​ c ​ e = 1 − 2 ​ ∑ i = 1 H ​ W Y ^ i ​ Y g ​ t , i + ϵ ∑ i = 1 H ​ W Y ^ i + ∑ i = 1 H ​ W Y g ​ t , i + ϵ . \mathcal{L}_{dice}=1-\frac{2\sum_{i=1}^{HW}\hat{Y}_{i}Y_{gt,i}+\epsilon}{\sum_{i=1}^{HW}\hat{Y}_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{HW}Y_{gt,i}+\epsilon}. (14) Here, ϵ \epsilon is a smoothing constant introduced to prevent numerical instability. While the segmentation loss supervises the final output, it does not explicitly enforce the semantic separation required for the effective operation of the Affinity-Driven Token Modulation module. To ensure that the global tokens used for prototype generation are semantically discriminative, we introduce a specialized prototype contrastive loss ℒ p ​ r ​ o ​ t ​ o \mathcal{L}_{proto} [ 44 ] . This loss acts as a regularizer that pulls foreground tokens towards the foreground prototype while pushing background tokens away from the background prototype in the feature space, thereby facilitating more accurate gating during the filtering process.

Given the set of normalized global tokens X ^ g ​ l ​ o ​ b ​ a ​ l ∈ ℝ N × C \hat{X}_{global}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C} and the dynamically computed prototypes P f P_{f} and P b P_{b} , the prototype contrastive loss is formulated as: ℒ p ​ r ​ o ​ t ​ o = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N [ Y g ​ t , i ⋅ d ⁡ ( X ^ g ​ l ​ o ​ b ​ a ​ l , i , P f ) + ( 1 − Y g ​ t , i ) ⋅ max ⁡ ( 0 , m − d ⁡ ( X ^ g ​ l ​ o ​ b ​ a ​ l , i , P b ) ) ] , \mathcal{L}_{proto}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[Y_{gt,i}\cdot d(\hat{X}_{global,i},P_{f})+(1-Y_{gt,i})\cdot\max(0,m-d(\hat{X}_{global,i},P_{b}))\right], (15) where d ⁡ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) d(\cdot,\cdot) represents the cosine distance metric, and m m is a hyperparameter margin. For foreground tokens (where Y g ​ t , i = 1 Y_{gt,i}=1 ), the loss minimizes the distance to the foreground prototype P f P_{f} . For background tokens (where Y g ​ t , i = 0 Y_{gt,i}=0 ), the loss minimizes a hinge term that encourages the distance to the background prototype P b P_{b} to be greater than the margin m m , ensuring a distinct separation between semantic classes. The final objective function for end-to-end training integrates the pixel-wise segmentation supervision with the semantic prototype regularization: ℒ t ​ o ​ t ​ a ​ l = ℒ s ​ e ​ g + λ ​ ℒ p ​ r ​ o ​ t ​ o , \mathcal{L}_{total}=\mathcal{L}_{seg}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{proto}, (16) where λ \lambda is a weighting coefficient that balances the contribution of the prototype loss. We empirically set λ \lambda to 0.1 to ensure that the contrastive learning provides sufficient semantic guidance without overwhelming the primary segmentation objective. 3.1 Overview of SDFA-Net Architecture SDFA-Net addresses thyroid nodule segmentation challenges by balancing local boundary delineation with global semantic understanding. The detailed formulation and implementation of each component are described in the following subsections. 4 Experiments 4.1 Datasets and Implementation Details We evaluated our approach on three public thyroid ultrasound benchmarks: TN3K [ 45 ] , DDTI [ 46 ] , and TUCC 1 1 1 https://stanfordaimi.azurewebsites.net/datasets/a72f2b02-7b53-4c5d-963c-d7253220bfd5 . TN3K, our primary dataset, comprises approximately 3,500 static images from 208 patients, covering a wide variety of nodule sizes and echogenicity patterns. We partitioned TN3K into training (70%), validation (10%), and test (20%) sets. The DDTI dataset, derived from 61 patient video sequences, was similarly partitioned (70/10/20) to maintain consistency. The TUCC dataset contains cine-clips acquired with different equipment and protocols, providing a complementary evaluation on data with distinct characteristics; it was also partitioned using the 70/10/20 split. All images were resized to 512 × 512 512\times 512 pixels and normalized. These datasets contain nodules with highly irregular boundaries, making them suitable benchmarks for boundary-sensitive segmentation. Quantitative assessment was performed using standard metrics that capture both volumetric overlap and boundary fidelity. The primary metric is the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), which measures the intersection between the predicted segmentation and the ground truth relative to their average size: DSC ​ ( P , G ) = 2 ​ | P ∩ G | | P | + | G | . \text{DSC}(P,G)=\frac{2|P\cap G|}{|P|+|G|}. (17) While DSC provides a global measure of segmentation accuracy, it can be insensitive to local boundary deviations. Therefore, we also utilized the 95th percentile Hausdorff Distance (HD95). HD95 calculates the maximum surface distance between the predicted and ground truth boundaries after removing the top 5% of outliers to ensure robustness against noise.

Lower HD95 values indicate better alignment with the actual nodule margin, which is particularly important for identifying spiculated or invasive boundaries associated with malignant tumors. The proposed framework was implemented using the PyTorch library and trained on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. We employed a ResNet-34, pre-trained on ImageNet [ 47 ] , as the backbone for the local feature extraction path to benefit from transfer learning from natural images, while the global context branch was initialized with random weights. The network was optimized end-to-end using the AdamW optimizer with an initial learning rate of 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} and a weight decay of 0.05. We employed a polynomial decay schedule to adjust the learning rate dynamically over 120 training epochs. The model was trained using a composite loss function combining Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) and Dice loss to handle class imbalance, supplemented by the prototype contrastive loss to enforce semantic discrimination. To enhance the model’s robustness to ultrasound imaging artifacts and orientation variations, we applied intensive data augmentation during training, including random rotations within the range of [ − 90 ∘ , 90 ∘ ] [-90^{\circ},90^{\circ}] , horizontal and vertical flipping, and random adjustments to brightness and contrast. Additionally, we utilized elastic deformations and Gaussian noise injection to simulate the speckle noise present in ultrasound imaging. The number of cluster centroids K K in the context aggregation module was set to 8, and the weight for the prototype loss λ \lambda was empirically set to 0.1. The final batch size was fixed at 16 to balance GPU memory consumption with training stability. 4.2 Ablation Studies We conduct comprehensive ablation studies on the primary dataset (TN3K) to validate the contribution of each proposed module, analyze design alternatives, and assess the sensitivity of key hyperparameters.

We employ solidity as a quantitative metric to measure shape irregularity, defined as the ratio of the nodule’s area to the area of its convex hull: solidity = Area ConvexHullArea \text{solidity}=\frac{\text{Area}}{\text{ConvexHullArea}} (18) where a value close to 1 indicates a regular, convex shape, while lower values signify irregular, lobulated, or spiculated boundaries commonly associated with malignancy [ 52 , 53 ] . We stratify the test samples from all three datasets into three equal-sized subgroups (Highly Irregular, Moderately Irregular, Regular) based on the terciles of their solidity scores. Similarly, we group nodules by size (Small, Medium, Large) based on the terciles of their pixel area, ensuring balanced sample sizes for robust statistical analysis. Figure 6 presents the Dice score distributions for each subgroup. As visually summarized in Figure 6 , SDFA-Net consistently outperforms all baseline methods across different solidity and size groups. In the “Highly Irregular” group, which represents the most challenging cases with complex boundaries, our method achieves a significant performance gain, validating the efficacy of the Spatially-Aligned Feature Fusion module in capturing fine-grained geometric details. Similarly, for “Small” nodules, SDFA-Net maintains high accuracy where other methods struggle due to limited spatial resolution. The consistent reduction in HD95 across all three datasets (Tables 6 - 8 ) further underscores the clinical relevance of our approach, as minimizing boundary errors is critical for reliable diagnosis. 4.1 Datasets and Implementation Details We evaluated our approach on three public thyroid ultrasound benchmarks: TN3K [ 45 ] , DDTI [ 46 ] , and TUCC 1 1 1 https://stanfordaimi.azurewebsites.net/datasets/a72f2b02-7b53-4c5d-963c-d7253220bfd5 . TN3K, our primary dataset, comprises approximately 3,500 static images from 208 patients, covering a wide variety of nodule sizes and echogenicity patterns.

We partitioned TN3K into training (70%), validation (10%), and test (20%) sets. The DDTI dataset, derived from 61 patient video sequences, was similarly partitioned (70/10/20) to maintain consistency. The TUCC dataset contains cine-clips acquired with different equipment and protocols, providing a complementary evaluation on data with distinct characteristics; it was also partitioned using the 70/10/20 split. All images were resized to 512 × 512 512\times 512 pixels and normalized. These datasets contain nodules with highly irregular boundaries, making them suitable benchmarks for boundary-sensitive segmentation. Quantitative assessment was performed using standard metrics that capture both volumetric overlap and boundary fidelity. The primary metric is the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), which measures the intersection between the predicted segmentation and the ground truth relative to their average size: DSC ​ ( P , G ) = 2 ​ | P ∩ G | | P | + | G | . \text{DSC}(P,G)=\frac{2|P\cap G|}{|P|+|G|}. (17) While DSC provides a global measure of segmentation accuracy, it can be insensitive to local boundary deviations. Therefore, we also utilized the 95th percentile Hausdorff Distance (HD95). HD95 calculates the maximum surface distance between the predicted and ground truth boundaries after removing the top 5% of outliers to ensure robustness against noise. Lower HD95 values indicate better alignment with the actual nodule margin, which is particularly important for identifying spiculated or invasive boundaries associated with malignant tumors. The proposed framework was implemented using the PyTorch library and trained on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. We employed a ResNet-34, pre-trained on ImageNet [ 47 ] , as the backbone for the local feature extraction path to benefit from transfer learning from natural images, while the global context branch was initialized with random weights.

The network was optimized end-to-end using the AdamW optimizer with an initial learning rate of 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} and a weight decay of 0.05. We employed a polynomial decay schedule to adjust the learning rate dynamically over 120 training epochs. The model was trained using a composite loss function combining Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) and Dice loss to handle class imbalance, supplemented by the prototype contrastive loss to enforce semantic discrimination. To enhance the model’s robustness to ultrasound imaging artifacts and orientation variations, we applied intensive data augmentation during training, including random rotations within the range of [ − 90 ∘ , 90 ∘ ] [-90^{\circ},90^{\circ}] , horizontal and vertical flipping, and random adjustments to brightness and contrast. Additionally, we utilized elastic deformations and Gaussian noise injection to simulate the speckle noise present in ultrasound imaging. The number of cluster centroids K K in the context aggregation module was set to 8, and the weight for the prototype loss λ \lambda was empirically set to 0.1. The final batch size was fixed at 16 to balance GPU memory consumption with training stability. 4.2 Ablation Studies We conduct comprehensive ablation studies on the primary dataset (TN3K) to validate the contribution of each proposed module, analyze design alternatives, and assess the sensitivity of key hyperparameters. 4.2.1 Component Ablations Table 1 presents a progressive evaluation of the core components in SDFA-Net.
